ns1:channel.ns1:title: Nature Human Behaviour
ns1:channel.ns1:description: Drawing from a broad spectrum of social and natural science disciplines, Nature Human Behaviour will publish research of outstanding significance into any aspect of human behaviour, its psychological, biological, and social bases. How do humans perceive, think, feel, decide, and act? How do they interact with their environments and others? How do these abilities develop and decline over the lifespan? How do they evolve and compare with other species? How do they vary among individuals, groups, and cultures? How are they shaped by socioeconomic and political factors? How are they affected by disease or deprivation? What interventions can influence individual behaviours or outcomes? The journal welcomes research from any discipline that provides significant original insight into these questions.

ns1:item.ns1:title: What chimpanzees at war have taught me about being human
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02601-6

Seeing a deadly ‘civil war’ unfold among chimpanzees has been a painful experience for John Mitani. His decades of watching wild great apes now evoke his family’s experience with xenophobia. But to him, the war highlights what makes humans unique: not our conflicts, but our unparalleled capacity for tolerance and cooperation.
ns1:item.dc:title: What chimpanzees at war have taught me about being human
ns1:item.dc:creator: John C. Mitani
ns1:item.dc:source: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 2026-09-21; | doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02601-6

ns1:item.ns1:title: There is no clear target for replication rates
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02602-5

Is a 50% replication rate too high, too low or just right? We need a target replication rate to answer this question. Here, I evaluate two potential target rates, the ‘optimal’ replication rate and the ‘expected’ replication rate, and I call for an educational intervention to better appreciate their limitations.
ns1:item.dc:title: There is no clear target for replication rates
ns1:item.dc:creator: Mark Rubin
ns1:item.dc:source: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 2026-09-21; | doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02602-5

ns1:item.ns1:title: Genome-wide analysis of social behaviour across social domains, reporters and developmental stages: a meta-regression approach
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 21 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02551-z

A genome-wide meta-regression analysis of social behaviour studying ~500,000 observations from ~70,000 individuals, modelling context-specific SNP variation as explained by social domains, informants and age, identified six associated loci.
ns1:item.dc:title: Genome-wide analysis of social behaviour across social domains, reporters and developmental stages: a meta-regression approach
